materials.title: My Morning
materials.body: I get up at six every morning. First, I open the window and drink a glass of water. Then I make coffee and read the news on my phone. I like quiet mornings, because I can think about my day. At seven, I have breakfast with my family. We eat bread, eggs and fruit. After breakfast, I study English for ten minutes. I say new words out loud and try to remember them. At eight, I leave home and walk to the station. It takes about fifteen minutes. On the way, I listen to an English story. It is a good start to the day.

questions.q: What does the writer do first in the morning?
options: Opens the window and drinks water

questions.q: How does the writer go to the station?

materials.title: A New Job
materials.body: Ken started a new job last month. He works for a small company that sells kitchen tools. On his first day, he was very nervous. He did not know anyone, and the office was big and busy. His manager, Ms. Brown, showed him around and introduced him to the team. Everyone was friendly. One woman, Lisa, helped him with the computer system. At lunch, they ate together and talked about their favorite food. Now Ken feels much better. He still makes some mistakes, but he is learning every day. He thinks the job is hard but interesting.

questions.q: What does Ken's company sell?
How does Ken feel about the job now?

materials.title: The Lost Umbrella
materials.body: Yesterday it rained all day. In the evening, I took the train home. I was very tired, so I sat down and closed my eyes. When I got off the train, the rain had stopped. I walked home happily. At home, I suddenly remembered my umbrella. I had left it on the train! It was a blue umbrella, a present from my sister. This morning, I called the station. A kind man said, "We have a blue umbrella. Please come and get it." I was so glad. Next time, I will hold my umbrella in my hand.

questions.q: Why did the writer forget the umbrella?
Who gave the umbrella to the writer?

materials.title: Weekend Plans
materials.body: Mika and her friend Sam are talking about the weekend. Sam wants to go to the beach on Saturday. Mika likes the idea, but the weather report says it will be cold and windy. So they change the plan. On Saturday, they will visit a new museum in the city. It has a special show about space. On Sunday, Mika will stay home. She wants to clean her room and cook a big meal for her parents. Sam will play football with his team in the afternoon. They both feel that a good weekend needs some fun and some rest.

questions.q: Why did they change the plan for Saturday?
options: The weather will be cold and windy

questions.q: What will Mika do on Sunday?

materials.title: At the Coffee Shop
materials.body: "Good morning. What can I get for you?" asked the young man at the counter. "A small coffee, please," said Emma. "Hot or iced?" "Hot, please. And could I have a piece of that cake?" "Of course. For here or to go?" "For here." "That will be six dollars." Emma paid with her card and sat by the window. The shop was warm and the music was soft. She opened her notebook and started to write a plan for her week. Coffee shops help her to think clearly. When she finished, she said "Thank you" to the young man and left with a smile.

questions.q: What did Emma order?
What did Emma do in the shop?
options: She wrote a plan for her week

materials.title: Learning a Little Every Day
materials.body: Tom wanted to learn the guitar. At first, he practiced for three hours every Sunday. But on Monday, he forgot most of it. He felt bad and almost stopped. Then his teacher gave him some advice: "Play for twenty minutes every day." Tom did not believe it would work, but he tried it. After one month, he could play three songs. After three months, he played at his friend's party. Everyone was surprised. Tom learned an important thing. A little practice every day is better than a lot of practice once a week.

questions.q: What was Tom's problem at first?
What is the main idea of the story?

materials.title: An Email to a New Client
materials.body: Dear Mr. Lee, Thank you for your call yesterday. It was a pleasure to talk with you about your plans for the new shop. As we discussed, our company can design and build the shelves and counters you need. I have attached a simple plan and a price list. The total cost would be about twelve thousand dollars, and the work would take three weeks. If the plan looks good to you, we could meet next Tuesday or Wednesday to talk about the details. Please let me know which day is better for you. I look forward to working with you. Best regards, Anna Sato

questions.q: What is the main purpose of this email?
options: To say sorry for a mistake
To send a plan and set up a meeting

questions.q: How long would the work take?

materials.title: A Short Team Meeting
materials.body: Every Monday at nine, our team has a short meeting. It only lasts fifteen minutes, and we all stand up. Our leader, David, asks three questions. What did you finish last week? What will you do this week? Is anything stopping your work? Each person answers in one or two minutes. If someone has a problem, we do not try to solve it in the meeting. Instead, two or three people talk about it later. At first, I thought the meeting was too short. But now I like it. Everyone knows what the others are doing, and we do not waste time.

questions.q: How long does the meeting last?
What happens when someone has a problem?
options: The whole team solves it in the meeting
A few people talk about it later

materials.title: Working from Home
materials.body: Since last year, Yuki has worked from home three days a week. At first, she loved it. She did not need to take a crowded train, and she had more time for breakfast. But after a few months, she found some problems. She often worked late because there was no clear end to the day. She also felt lonely, because she could not chat with her co-workers. So Yuki made some rules for herself. She starts at nine and stops at six. She takes a walk at lunch. Once a week, she has a video call with a co-worker just to talk. Now she enjoys working from home again.

questions.q: What problem did Yuki have?
options: She worked late and felt lonely

questions.q: Which is one of Yuki's rules?

materials.title: Giving a Presentation
materials.body: Next Friday, Leo has to give his first presentation in English. He will talk to a group of customers about a new product. He is worried, because his English is not perfect. His friend Maria gave him some useful tips. First, keep the slides simple, with only a few words on each one. Second, practice out loud many times, and record yourself. Third, speak slowly and pause after important points. Finally, it is fine to make small mistakes. People care more about the message than about perfect grammar. Leo feels a little better now. He has started to practice every evening.

questions.q: Who will listen to Leo's presentation?
According to Maria, what do people care about most?

materials.title: The Night Market
materials.body: When I visited Taiwan last spring, my favorite place was a night market. It opened at six in the evening and stayed busy until midnight. There were hundreds of small stands selling food, clothes and toys. The air was full of smells: fried chicken, sweet potatoes, and a famous strong-smelling tofu. I was a little afraid of the tofu, but a friendly woman at the stand told me to try it. To my surprise, it was delicious. I also played a simple game and won a small toy. Walking through the bright, noisy market, I felt that I was really part of the city.

questions.q: When did the market open?
How did the writer feel about the tofu after trying it?

materials.title: Why We Forget
materials.body: Have you ever learned a new word and forgotten it the next day? This is very normal. More than a hundred years ago, a German scientist named Hermann Ebbinghaus studied memory. He found that we forget most new information within a day or two. But he also found good news. Each time we review the information, we forget it more slowly. So the best way to learn is to review new words several times, with longer and longer breaks between each review: after one day, then three days, then a week, and so on. Many language apps today use this simple idea.

questions.q: What did Ebbinghaus study?
What is the best way to remember new words, according to the text?
options: Study them once for a long time
Review them with longer and longer breaks

materials.title: A Good Email
materials.body:
Many people at work read more than a hundred emails a day. So a good email must be short and clear. First, write a subject line that tells the reader what the email is about. For example, "Meeting on Friday: new time" is better than "Hello".

In the first sentence, say what you want. Do you need an answer, a decision, or only want to share news? Then give the details. Use short paragraphs, and use a list if you have several points.

At the end, say clearly what should happen next and by when. For example, "Could you send me the report by Thursday?" Before you press send, read the email once more. Check the names, the dates, and the numbers. A small mistake can cause a big problem.

questions.q: What should the first sentence of an email do?
options: Say hello in a friendly way

questions.q: What should you check before you send an email?
options: How many emails you sent today

materials.title: Working from Home
materials.body:
Since 2020, many companies have let their workers work from home. Some people love it. They do not have to travel to the office, so they save time and money. They can also focus better because the office is often noisy.

But working from home is not easy for everyone. Some people feel lonely. They miss talking with their coworkers over lunch. Others find it hard to stop working, because their office is also their home.

Today, many companies use a mix. Workers come to the office two or three days a week and work from home on the other days. Managers say this helps people work together and still keep a good balance between work and life. The best plan is different for each team, so it is important to talk about it openly.

questions.q: Why do some people find it hard to stop working at home?
options: Their manager calls them at night
Their office is also their home

questions.q: What do many companies do today?
options: They use a mix of office and home
They make everyone work from home
They make everyone come to the office

materials.title: How a Meeting Should Work
materials.body:
Meetings take a lot of time, so a good meeting needs a plan. Before the meeting, the leader sends an agenda. The agenda lists the topics and how long each one will take. People can prepare, and they know why they are there.

During the meeting, one person keeps time and another person takes notes. The leader makes sure everyone can speak, not only the loudest people. If a topic takes too long, the leader can move it to another day.

At the end, the group agrees on the next steps. Who will do what, and by when? Within a day, the note taker sends a short summary to everyone. Many experts say that if a meeting has no clear goal, it should be an email instead.

questions.q: What is an agenda?
options: A list of people who are late
A list of topics and times
A summary of the last meeting

questions.q: What do many experts say about a meeting with no clear goal?
options: It should be an email instead

materials.title: The Customer Is Talking
materials.body:
A coffee shop owner wanted to know why sales were falling. She did not guess. She asked her customers. For two weeks, she put a small card on every table with one question: "What would make you come here more often?"

She got over two hundred answers. Many people said the coffee was good, but the line in the morning was too long. Some said they wanted a place to charge their phones.

So she made two changes. She let customers order on an app before they arrived, and she added power outlets near the windows. Three months later, morning sales were up by twenty percent. "The answers were there all the time," she said. "I only had to ask."

questions.q: What was the main problem in the morning?
What happened three months after the changes?
options: Morning sales went up by 20 percent

materials.title: What Is Inflation?
materials.body:
Inflation means that prices in general go up over time. If a cup of coffee costs three dollars this year and three dollars and fifteen cents next year, its price has risen by five percent. When most prices rise like this, the same amount of money buys less.

A little inflation is normal. Many central banks try to keep it at about two percent a year. When inflation is too high, people and businesses find it hard to plan. Workers may need higher pay just to buy the same things.

To slow inflation, a central bank can raise interest rates. Then borrowing money becomes more expensive, so people and companies spend less. When spending falls, prices usually rise more slowly. But if rates go up too much, the economy can slow down too much.

questions.q: What level of inflation do many central banks aim for?
Why do higher interest rates slow inflation?
options: Borrowing costs more, so people spend less
They make prices fall at once

materials.title: The First Day at a New Job
materials.body:
Ryo started his first job at a trading company in April. On the first day, he felt nervous. He arrived twenty minutes early and waited in the lobby.

His manager, Ms. Lee, showed him around the office. She introduced him to the team and gave him a laptop and an ID card. Then she gave him a list of things to learn in the first month. "Nobody expects you to know everything," she said. "If you are not sure, ask. A question now saves a mistake later."

At lunch, two coworkers took him to a noodle shop nearby. They told him which meetings were important and which ones he could skip. By the end of the day, Ryo was tired but happy. He wrote down three things he had learned and went home early to rest.

questions.q: What did Ms. Lee tell Ryo to do when he is not sure?
What did Ryo do at the end of the day?
options: He stayed late to finish work
He went out with the team
He wrote down three things he learned

materials.title: Small Talk
materials.body:
Small talk is a short, friendly conversation about easy topics. In business, it often happens before a meeting starts or during a coffee break. It may seem unimportant, but it helps people feel comfortable and builds trust.

Good topics for small talk are the weather, travel, food, and weekend plans. For example, you can ask, "Did you have a good trip here?" or "Have you tried any good restaurants nearby?" Topics like money, religion, and politics are usually best avoided.

The key is to ask open questions and listen. An open question cannot be answered with only yes or no. Instead of "Do you like Tokyo?", try "What do you like about Tokyo?" Then show interest in the answer and add a little about yourself. A few minutes of small talk can make the real meeting go much better.

questions.q: Which topic is usually best avoided in small talk?
Which is an open question?
options: What do you like about Tokyo?

materials.title: Why Startups Fail
materials.body:
Every year, thousands of new companies start with big dreams. But many of them close within five years. Why?

One study looked at more than a hundred failed startups. The most common reason was simple: there was no market need. The founders built a product that they liked, but not enough customers wanted to pay for it. The second reason was running out of money. The third was having the wrong team.

Successful founders often do something different at the start. Before they build the full product, they talk to possible customers and test a simple version. If people do not want it, they change the idea quickly. This is sometimes called a "pivot". Failing early and cheaply, they say, is much better than failing late and expensively.

questions.q: What was the most common reason startups failed?
What is a "pivot"?

materials.title: Giving a Presentation
materials.body:
Many people are afraid of speaking in front of a group. But a good presentation is a skill, and anyone can learn it.

Start with your goal. What do you want the audience to know or do at the end? Build your talk around one main message, and support it with three points at most. People cannot remember ten points.

Keep your slides simple. Use a few words and a clear picture or chart on each slide. If your slides are full of text, people will read instead of listening to you.

Finally, practice out loud, not only in your head. Time yourself. Ask a friend to listen and tell you which part was unclear. On the day, speak a little slower than normal and look at the people, not at the screen. If you make a mistake, smile and keep going.

questions.q: How many supporting points does the writer suggest?
What happens if slides are full of text?

materials.title: The Supply Chain
materials.body:
Think about a smartphone. Its parts come from many countries. The screen may be made in Korea, the chips in Taiwan, and the battery in China. The parts are put together in one factory, and then the phones are shipped all over the world. This whole system is called a supply chain.

A supply chain can save money, because each step happens where it is cheapest or best. But it can also break. In 2021, a large ship got stuck in the Suez Canal for six days. Hundreds of other ships had to wait, and many shops ran out of goods.

Since then, many companies have changed their plans. They buy parts from more than one supplier, and they keep more inventory. This costs more, but it makes the business safer when something goes wrong.

questions.q: What happened in the Suez Canal in 2021?
options: The canal was closed for a year

questions.q: What have many companies done since then?
options: Bought parts from more than one supplier

materials.title: Business Cards in Japan
materials.body:
In Japan, exchanging business cards is an important part of meeting someone for the first time. Visitors from other countries are often surprised by how careful people are.

You hold your card with both hands, with the text facing the other person so they can read it. You say your company name and your own name, and give a small bow. When you receive a card, you also use both hands and take a moment to read it.

During a meeting, people often place the cards on the table in front of them, in the same order as the people sitting there. This helps them remember names. It is not polite to write on someone's card or to put it in your back pocket. After the meeting, you put the cards carefully in a card case. A card is treated as part of the person.

questions.q: How do people hold a business card when giving it?
Why do people place cards on the table during a meeting?

materials.title: The Power of Feedback
materials.body:
Feedback is information about how well someone is doing. Good feedback helps people grow, but bad feedback can make them angry or sad.

One simple method is to describe the situation, the behavior, and the impact. For example: "In yesterday's meeting with the client, you explained the price very clearly. Because of that, they agreed quickly." This is much more useful than "Good job." It tells the person exactly what to keep doing.

The same method works for problems. "In this morning's report, three numbers were wrong. Because of that, the manager had to check everything again." It talks about the work, not the person.

Feedback should also be timely. If you wait a month, people forget the details. And remember that feedback goes both ways. A good manager often asks, "What could I do better?"

questions.q: What are the three parts of the simple method?
Why should feedback be timely?

materials.title: Exchange Rates
materials.body:
An exchange rate is the price of one currency in another currency. For example, if one US dollar buys 150 yen, the exchange rate is 150 yen to the dollar.

Exchange rates change every day. When the yen gets weaker, one dollar buys more yen. This is good news for Japanese companies that sell goods abroad, because their products become cheaper for foreign buyers. It is also good for tourism, because Japan becomes a cheaper place to visit.

But a weak yen has a downside. Japan imports a lot of oil, food, and other goods. When the yen is weak, these imports cost more, so prices in Japanese shops go up. For people who want to travel overseas, a weak yen also means that hotels and meals abroad feel more expensive.

questions.q: Who benefits when the yen gets weaker?
options: Japanese companies that sell goods abroad

questions.q: Why do prices in Japanese shops go up when the yen is weak?

materials.title: A Late Shipment
materials.body:
Mika works in customer service for an online furniture shop. One morning, a customer called. He had ordered a desk for his new home office, but it had not arrived. It was three days late.

Mika checked the order. The desk was stuck at a warehouse because of a storm. She could have said, "It is not our fault." Instead, she said, "I am very sorry. I understand you need it for work." She explained what had happened and gave him a new delivery date.

Then she did one more thing. She offered free delivery on his next order. The customer thanked her and later wrote a good review. "The desk was late," he wrote, "but the service was excellent." Mika's manager shared the review with the whole team as an example of how to handle problems.

questions.q: Why was the desk late?
options: The customer gave the wrong address
It was stuck at a warehouse because of a storm

questions.q: What did Mika offer the customer?
options: Free delivery on his next order

materials.title: Time Zones and Teams
materials.body:
Kenji works for a software company in Osaka. His team has members in London and San Francisco. When it is nine in the morning in Osaka, it is midnight in London and five in the afternoon of the day before in San Francisco.

At first, the team tried to meet every day. Someone always had to join very early or very late, and people got tired. So they changed their way of working.

Now they meet only twice a week, at a time that is fair to most people. On other days, they write updates in a shared document. Each person writes what they did, what they will do next, and any problems. Because of the time difference, work can move forward almost all day. When Kenji goes to bed, his coworkers in London are just starting their day.

questions.q: Why did the team stop meeting every day?
options: Someone always had to join very early or late

questions.q: What do team members write in the shared document?
options: What they did, what they will do, and problems

materials.title: Price and Value
materials.body:
Why will people pay five dollars for a coffee at one café but only one dollar at a convenience store? The coffee may be similar, but the value is different.

Value is what customers feel they get for their money. At the café, they get a comfortable chair, free Wi-Fi, a nice smell, and a place to meet friends. For many people, that is worth the extra four dollars.

Companies can set prices in several ways. Some start with their costs and add a profit. Others look at what competitors charge. But many successful companies start with value. They ask, "What is this worth to the customer?" A product that saves a business a lot of time can have a high price, even if it was cheap to make. The trick is to understand what the customer really cares about.

questions.q: According to the text, what is value?
options: What customers feel they get for their money
The cost of making a product

questions.q: What question do many successful companies ask?
options: What is this worth to the customer?
How cheap can we make it?

materials.title: The Job Interview
materials.body:
A job interview is a conversation, not a test. The company wants to know if you can do the job and if you will fit in the team. You also want to know if the company is right for you.

Prepare by reading about the company. What does it sell? Who are its customers? What news has there been recently? Then think of stories from your own experience. For a question like "Tell me about a time you solved a problem," a short story works well. Describe the situation, what you did, and the result.

At the end, the interviewer usually asks, "Do you have any questions?" Always have one or two ready. For example, "What does a successful first year look like in this role?" A good question shows that you are serious and that you have thought about the job.

questions.q: What should you do before the interview?
options: Memorize your résumé word for word

questions.q: What should you do when asked "Do you have any questions?"
options: Ask one or two prepared questions

materials.title: Saying No Politely
materials.body:
At work, people often ask you to do more than you can. Saying yes to everything may seem kind, but it can lead to late nights, poor work, and stress.

Saying no politely is a useful skill. First, thank the person for asking. Then explain your situation briefly. For example: "Thanks for thinking of me. Right now I am working on the sales report, and it is due on Friday."

Next, offer another option if you can. "I could help next week," or "Maybe Sarah has time? She knows this area well." You can also ask your manager to choose: "Which is more important, the report or this new task?"

This way, you are not simply refusing. You are helping the team use its time well. Most people respect someone who is honest about what they can do.

questions.q: What is the first step in saying no politely?
What does the writer suggest you can ask your manager?

materials.title: Reading a Profit and Loss Statement
materials.body:
A profit and loss statement shows how much money a company made and spent in a period, such as a quarter or a year. It is also called an income statement.

At the top is revenue, the money from sales. Below that is the cost of goods sold, which is what it cost to make or buy the products. Revenue minus the cost of goods sold is the gross profit.

Next come operating expenses, like salaries, rent, and advertising. When you subtract these, you get operating profit. This number shows how well the main business is doing. Finally, after interest and taxes, you reach net profit, the famous "bottom line".

Investors look at more than the bottom line. A company can show a profit because it sold a building, even if its main business is weak. That is why operating profit is so important.

questions.q: What is gross profit?
options: Revenue minus the cost of goods sold

questions.q: Why is operating profit important?
options: It includes the sale of buildings
It shows how well the main business is doing
It is always the largest number

materials.title: The Elevator Pitch
materials.body:
Imagine you get into an elevator with an important investor. You have about thirty seconds before the doors open. What would you say? This short speech is called an elevator pitch.

A good pitch answers three questions. What problem do you solve? Who has this problem? And why is your solution better? For example: "Small restaurants waste a lot of food because they cannot predict how many customers will come. Our app uses past sales and the weather to predict demand. Our first ten customers cut their food waste by a third."

Notice the numbers at the end. They make the pitch believable. Avoid difficult words and long explanations. The goal is not to tell everything. The goal is to make the listener say, "Tell me more."

questions.q: How long is an elevator pitch, according to the text?
What is the goal of an elevator pitch?
options: To make the listener want to know more
To sell the product at once
To tell everything about the business

materials.title: Taking Notes in Meetings
materials.body:
Taking good notes in a meeting is harder than it looks. Many people try to write down every word, but then they miss what is really happening.

A better way is to listen for three things: decisions, actions, and open questions. A decision is something the group has agreed on. An action is a task with a person's name and a deadline. An open question is something that still needs an answer.

You can draw three columns on your page, or use three letters: D, A, and Q. When you hear "OK, let's go with plan B," write it under D. When you hear "Tom will call the supplier by Monday," write it under A.

After the meeting, clean up your notes while your memory is fresh. Then share them. Your coworkers will thank you.

questions.q: What three things should you listen for?
Which is an example of an action?
options: Tom will call the supplier by Monday

materials.title: A Family Business
materials.body:
In the city of Kyoto, there is a sweets shop that has been open for more than four hundred years. It has been run by the same family for eighteen generations. Japan has more very old companies than any other country. Some are over a thousand years old.

Why do they last so long? Experts point to a few reasons. They focus on one thing and do it very well. They care more about trust and long-term relationships than about growing fast. And they keep money aside for hard times, so they can survive wars, disasters, and recessions.

But old companies also change. The sweets shop now sells online and has created new flavors for younger customers. The current owner says, "To protect our tradition, we must keep changing a little every year."

questions.q: How long has the sweets shop been open?
What does the current owner say about tradition?
options: To protect it, they must keep changing a little
It is not important to young people

materials.title: Negotiation Basics
materials.body:
Negotiation is not a fight. It is a way for two sides to find an agreement that works for both.

Before you negotiate, know your BATNA. This stands for "best alternative to a negotiated agreement". In other words, what will you do if you cannot agree? If you have a good alternative, you can negotiate with more confidence.

During the negotiation, focus on interests, not positions. A position is what someone says they want, such as "We need a lower price." An interest is why they want it, such as "Our budget is small this year." If you understand the interest, you may find other solutions. For example, you could keep the price but let them pay over six months.

Finally, listen more than you talk. The more you know about the other side, the better deal you can make.

questions.q: What does BATNA mean?
options: The lowest price you will accept
Your best alternative if you cannot agree

questions.q: What is the difference between a position and an interest?
options: A position is what someone wants; an interest is why
A position is why; an interest is what

materials.title: Marketing to the Right People
materials.body:
A small company that makes running shoes had a problem. It spent a lot of money on advertising, but sales did not grow. The ads were shown to everyone, from teenagers to grandparents.

So the company changed its approach. It studied its best customers and found that most of them were adults aged 30 to 50 who ran long distances on weekends. Many of them cared about avoiding injuries.

The company stopped showing ads to everyone. Instead, it put ads in running magazines and on running apps. The message also changed: "Run longer without pain." The company even sponsored local marathons. Within a year, sales doubled, and the advertising budget was actually smaller. The lesson is simple. You do not need to reach everyone. You need to reach the right people with the right message.

questions.q: Who were most of the company's best customers?
options: Adults aged 30 to 50 who ran long distances

questions.q: What happened within a year?
options: The ads were shown to everyone again
Sales doubled with a smaller budget

materials.title: The Weekly Report
materials.body:
Every Friday, Emma writes a short weekly report for her manager. At first, she wrote long reports that described everything she did. Her manager rarely read them to the end.

Then a senior coworker gave her advice. "Your manager has twenty minutes for twenty reports," she said. "Put the most important thing first."

Now Emma uses a simple format with four parts. First, one sentence on the overall status: on track, at risk, or delayed. Second, three main results from the week. Third, any problems and what help she needs. Fourth, the plan for next week.

The report now fits on one screen. Her manager reads it every week and often replies within an hour. Last month, she even asked Emma to teach the format to the rest of the team.

questions.q: What was the problem with Emma's first reports?
options: They were too long and not read to the end

questions.q: What comes first in Emma's new format?
options: One sentence on the overall status

materials.title: What Is a Stock?
materials.body:
When you buy a stock, or a share, you buy a very small part of a company. If the company has one million shares and you own one thousand, you own one tenth of one percent of it.

There are two main ways to make money from stocks. First, the price of the share can go up. If you buy at ten dollars and sell at fifteen, you make five dollars per share. Second, many companies pay a dividend, which is a part of their profit paid to shareholders.

Of course, prices can also go down. A company can lose customers or make bad decisions. That is why many people buy funds that hold many different stocks. If one company does badly, the others may still do well. Experts often say that stocks are best for money you will not need for many years.

materials.title: Cross-Cultural Communication
materials.body:
A Japanese manager and an American manager were working on a project together. In a meeting, the American asked, "Can we finish this by the end of the month?" The Japanese manager said, "It may be difficult." The American heard "It is possible, but hard." The Japanese manager meant "No."

This kind of misunderstanding is common. Some cultures, like the United States and Germany, often say things directly. Other cultures, like Japan, often expect the listener to understand the meaning from the situation.

Neither way is wrong. But in an international team, it helps to be clear. You can check by asking, "Just to be sure, does that mean we cannot finish by the end of the month?" You can also explain your own style: "In Japan, we often say 'difficult' when we mean 'no'." Small steps like these prevent big problems.

materials.title: The Coffee Chain That Listened
materials.body:
A large coffee chain was losing customers to small local cafés. Its stores were clean and fast, but customers said they felt like factories.

The company asked store managers for ideas. One manager suggested letting each store choose some of its own decorations and a few local products. Another suggested training staff to remember regular customers' names and usual orders.

The company tested these ideas in fifty stores. After six months, the test stores had more regular customers than other stores, and staff were happier too. Many said they enjoyed their work more because they could make real connections.

The company then spread the ideas to all its stores. The chief executive later said, "Our best ideas did not come from headquarters. They came from people who talk to customers every day."

materials.title: Managing Your Time
materials.body:
Many busy people feel that they work all day but do not finish anything important. One reason is that urgent tasks push out important ones.

An urgent task needs attention now, like a ringing phone. An important task helps you reach your long-term goals, like learning a new skill or planning next year's budget. Some tasks are both, some are neither.

A useful habit is to plan your day the evening before. Choose one important task and do it first, before you check email. Even sixty minutes of focused work in the morning can make a big difference.

Also, group small tasks together. Answer emails two or three times a day instead of every few minutes. Every time you switch tasks, your brain needs time to focus again. Fewer switches mean more real work.

materials.title: Electric Cars and Business
materials.body:
Electric cars are changing more than how we drive. They are changing whole industries.

A normal car engine has hundreds of moving parts. An electric motor has far fewer. This is bad news for companies that make engine parts, and many of them must find new products. On the other hand, battery makers are growing fast. Batteries are the most expensive part of an electric car, so companies are racing to make them cheaper and better.

Electric cars also need charging stations. Some oil companies now build chargers at their gas stations. Electricity companies sell special plans for charging at night, when power is cheaper. Even shopping malls add chargers, hoping drivers will shop while they wait. When technology changes, some businesses lose, but new chances appear for those who move quickly.

materials.title: A Difficult Client
materials.body:
Daniel worked at a design company. His newest client changed the plan almost every week. First she wanted blue, then green, then blue again. The project was already two weeks late, and the team was frustrated.

Daniel decided to meet her in person. Instead of complaining, he asked questions. "What is most important to you in this design? Who will see it?" He learned that her boss kept giving her new opinions, and she was under a lot of pressure.

So Daniel suggested a new process. The team would make two options. She would show both to her boss, and they would choose one together within three days. After that, changes would cost extra.

The client agreed and even seemed relieved. The project finished one week later. The next year, she hired Daniel's company again.

materials.title: The Gig Economy
materials.body:
In the gig economy, people work on short jobs, or "gigs", instead of having one long-term employer. A driver may take rides through an app, a designer may find projects online, and a translator may work for clients in ten countries.

For workers, gigs offer freedom. They can choose when and how much to work. Some people do gigs on top of a regular job to earn extra money.

But there are risks. Gig workers often do not get paid holidays, sick pay, or pensions. Their income can change a lot from month to month. In many countries, governments are discussing new rules to protect them.

For companies, gig workers make it easy to grow or shrink quickly. But some companies have found that people who feel secure in their jobs work harder and stay longer.

materials.title: Why Prices End in 99
materials.body:
Have you noticed that many prices end in 99? A shirt costs 19.99 dollars, not 20. A meal costs 980 yen, not 1,000.

This is not an accident. Studies show that people read prices from left to right and pay most attention to the first number. So 19.99 feels closer to 10 than to 20, even though the difference from 20 is only one cent.

But some shops do the opposite on purpose. Expensive restaurants and luxury brands often use round numbers like 50 or 200. Round numbers feel simple and confident, and they suggest quality rather than a good deal.

So the price tag sends a message. A price ending in 99 says "This is a bargain." A round price says "This is premium." Next time you go shopping, see which message each shop is sending.

materials.title: Learning from Mistakes
materials.body:
Some companies punish people for mistakes. As a result, workers hide problems until it is too late. Other companies treat mistakes as chances to learn.

After a project, these companies hold a short meeting called a review. The team asks four questions. What did we expect to happen? What actually happened? Why was there a difference? What will we do differently next time?

The key rule is that the review is about the process, not about blaming a person. If a report was late, the question is not "Who was lazy?" but "What in our process made it late?" Maybe the deadline was unclear, or one person had too much work.

Airlines and hospitals have used this method for many years. When people feel safe to talk about mistakes, the same mistakes happen less often.

On the second day, Aya visited shops to see how kitchen products were sold. She noticed that many families cooked in small kitchens, so compact products were popular.

On the last day, she wrote a report on the plane. She recommended the smaller distributor and suggested making a smaller version of their best-selling pan for the local market.

materials.title: Your Personal Brand
materials.body:
A personal brand is what people think of when they hear your name at work. Are you the person who always meets deadlines? The person who explains things clearly? The person who brings new ideas?

You build your brand through your actions every day, not through a single big success. Small things matter: answering emails on time, being prepared for meetings, and keeping your promises.

It also helps to share what you know. You could give a short talk to your team about a tool you have learned, or write a useful guide for new staff. People will start to see you as an expert in that area.

Finally, be consistent. If you are helpful on Monday but rude on Friday, people will not know what to expect. Trust grows slowly, but it is one of the most valuable things you can have in your career.

Sales, I think. I enjoy meeting people like you.
That's very kind. Next time you come to London, dinner is on me.
materials.body:
Mr. Evans: Thank you for inviting me to such a nice restaurant, Kana.

Kana: It's our pleasure. Have you tried Japanese food like this before?

Mr. Evans: Only sushi in London. This is my first time trying tempura in Japan.

Kana: I hope you enjoy it. This restaurant is famous for its fresh vegetables.

Mr. Evans: It's delicious. How long have you worked with your company?

Kana: About six years. I started in the finance team and moved to sales two years ago.

Mr. Evans: Interesting. Which do you like better?

Kana: Sales, I think. I enjoy meeting people like you.

Mr. Evans: That's very kind. Next time you come to London, dinner is on me.

Kana: I'll hold you to that!

questions.q: What is Mr. Evans trying for the first time in Japan?
Which team did Kana start in?

materials.title: Ending a Project
materials.scene: プロジェクトの振り返り
lines: The project is finished. Let's look back. What went well?
We finished on time, and the client was very happy with the result.
I think our daily fifteen-minute meetings helped a lot. Everyone knew what others were doing.
Agreed. And what could we do better next time?
We spent too much time on the first design. We should show the client simple drafts earlier.
Also, the testing was rushed at the end. We need more time for it in the plan.
Good points. So next time: show drafts early and plan more time for testing.
Should we write this down for other teams?
Yes. I'll share a short summary with the department.
Thanks, everyone. It was a great team.
materials.body:

Mio: Should we write this down for other teams?

Leader: Yes. I'll share a short summary with the department.

Jack: Thanks, everyone. It was a great team.

questions.q: What helped the team, according to Jack?
What will they do differently next time?
options: Show drafts early and plan more time for testing

materials.title: Internet
materials.body:
The Internet is the world’s largest global communication network for computers and other devices.

It connects many smaller networks from homes, schools, businesses, and governments. These networks share different kinds of information. The short form of the Internet is “the Net.” One of its most popular services is the World Wide Web, which is used by billions of people every day.

The Internet was developed in the United States by the Department of Defence Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA). The Internet was first connected in October 1969 and was called ARPANET. The World Wide Web was created at CERN in Switzerland in 1990 by a British (UK) scientist named Tim Berners-Lee.

questions.q: Where was the World Wide Web created?
options: At a university in the UK

questions.q: What was the Internet called when it was first connected in 1969?

materials.source: Simple English Wikipedia「Internet」（版 11007339 の冒頭を抜粋）

materials.title: Elephant
materials.body:
Elephants are the biggest living land mammals. They have long noses called trunks and large flapping ears. The largest elephant ever recorded was shot in Angola in 1974. It weighed 27,060 lb (12.27 t) and stood 13 ft 8 in (4.17 m) tall.

At birth, an elephant calf may be as big as 100 kg (225 pounds). The baby elephant develops for 20 to 22 months inside its mother. No other land animal takes this long to develop before being born.

In the wild, elephants have strong family relationships. Their ways of acting toward other elephants are hard for people to understand. They "talk" to each other with very low sounds. Most elephants sounds are so low, people cannot hear them. But elephants can hear these sounds from very far away.

Elephants have strong, leathery skin to protect themselves.

questions.q: How long does a baby elephant develop inside its mother?
Why can't people hear most elephant sounds?
options: They are too quiet in the day

materials.source: Simple English Wikipedia「Elephant」（版 10879973 の冒頭を抜粋）

materials.title: Bicycle
materials.body:
A bicycle (or bike) is a small, human powered land vehicle with a seat, two wheels, two pedals, and a metal chain connected to cogs on the pedals and rear wheel. A frame gives the bike strength, and the other parts are attached to the frame. The name comes from the prefix bi (meaning two) and the suffix cycle (meaning wheel). It is powered by a person riding on top, who pushes the pedals around with his or her feet.

Riding bicycles, which is also called cycling, is an important way to travel in several parts of the world. The most popular type of cycling is Utility cycling. It is also a common kind of recreation, a good form of low-impact exercise, and a popular sport. According to one study, road bicycle racing is the eighth most popular spectator sport in the world.

Cycling uses less energy per mile than any other human transport.

questions.q: What does 'bi' in 'bicycle' mean?
What is true about cycling, according to the text?
options: It uses less energy per mile than any other human transport
It is the most popular sport to watch

materials.source: Simple English Wikipedia「Bicycle」（版 10911070 の冒頭を抜粋）

materials.title: Coffee
materials.body:
Coffee is a caffeinated drink prepared from roasted coffee beans. It's also a plant (Coffea) and the name of the drink that is made from this plant. The coffee plant is a bush or tree that can grow up to ten meters (about 32 feet) high, but is usually cut shorter. Coffee plants originally grew in Ethiopia, and now also grow in South America, Central America, Southeast Asia and Turkey. They are an important crop for the economies of many countries.

The drink is made from the seeds of the coffee plant, called coffee beans. Coffee is usually served hot, and is a popular drink in many countries.

To make a drink from coffee beans, the beans must first be specially prepared by drying the beans and then roasting. The beans are dried a short time after they are picked. This preserves them and makes them ready to be packed or roasted. Before the beans are made into a drink, they must be roasted and ground (crushed into tiny pieces in a coffee mill). When the ground coffee is placed into boiling water, the flavour and dark brown colour of the beans goes into the water. Making coffee is called brewing coffee. There are several different ways that coffee can be brewed.

questions.q: Where did coffee plants first grow?
What must happen to coffee beans before they are made into a drink?

materials.source: Simple English Wikipedia「Coffee」（版 10958734 の冒頭を抜粋）

materials.title: Olympic Games
materials.body:
The Olympic Games (French: Jeux olympiques) is an important international event featuring summer and winter sports. Summer Olympic Games and Winter Olympic Games are held every four years. Originally, the ancient Olympic Games were held in Ancient Greece at Olympia. The first games were in 776 BC. They were held every four years until the 6th century AC. The first "modern" Olympics took place in 1896 in Athens, Greece. Athletes participate in the Olympics Games to represent their countries.

Over time the Olympics have become bigger. In old times, women were not allowed, but now there are women's events. The Winter Games were created for ice and snow sports. The Paralympic Games were created for athletes with physical disabilities. As well, the Olympics became bigger with the addition of the Youth Olympic Games for teenage athletes. World War I and World War II led to the cancellation of the 1916, 1940, and 1944 Games. As the decision-making body, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) is responsible for choosing the host city for each Olympic Games. The IOC is also responsible for choosing what sports are in the games. The creator of modern Olympics is Baron Pierre de Coubertin.

questions.q: Where were the first modern Olympics held?
Why were the 1916, 1940 and 1944 Games cancelled?

materials.source: Simple English Wikipedia「Olympic Games」（版 10966461 の冒頭を抜粋）

materials.title: Telephone
materials.body: A telephone, also known as a phone, is a communication tool. People use it to talk with people far away. Originally, it was an electric tool sending analogue speech through wires. Many telephones in the 21st century are electronic tools sending digital signals on wires or radio transmission. Using a telephone, two people who are in different places can talk to each other. Early telephones needed to be connected with wires which are called fixed or landline telephones. Modern mobile phones use radio waves.

questions.q: What do modern mobile phones use?
What were early telephones that needed wires called?

materials.source: Simple English Wikipedia「Telephone」（版 10939880 の冒頭を抜粋）

materials.title: Chocolate
materials.body:
Chocolate is a food made from cacao beans. It is used in many desserts like pudding, cakes, candy, ice cream, and Easter eggs. It can be in a solid form like a candy bar or it can be in a liquid form like hot chocolate. Commercial chocolate has sugar and sometimes milk added. It has a melting point of about 30 to 32 °C (86 to 90 °F).

Dark chocolate has less sugar, and a more bitter taste. It was originally used to make drinking chocolate. Chocolate has been around the world since the time of the Olmec, Mayan, and Aztecs.

questions.q: What is chocolate made from?
How is dark chocolate different?
options: It has less sugar and tastes more bitter
It melts at a higher temperature

materials.source: Simple English Wikipedia「Chocolate」（版 10910651 の冒頭を抜粋）

materials.title: Mount Fuji
materials.body: Mount Fuji (富士山, Fuji-san) is the tallest mountain in Japan, at 3,776 metres (12,388 ft) high. It is also a volcano. It is on the border between Shizuoka Prefecture and Yamanashi Prefecture. Mount Fuji is a famous cultural icon of Japan, as a lot of people have painted it and taken photographs of it. It became the 13th UNESCO World Heritage Site in Japan on June 22, 2013. The last time it erupted was from 1707 to 1708.

questions.q: How high is Mount Fuji?
When did Mount Fuji last erupt?

materials.source: Simple English Wikipedia「Mount Fuji」（版 10393922 の冒頭を抜粋）

materials.title: Moon
materials.body:
The Moon, also known as Luna, is Earth's only natural satellite (the only object which orbits the Earth and is not man-made). It is usually visible in the night sky, but is sometimes seen during the day.

The Moon is about one-fourth of the width of Earth. Because it is so far away it looks small in the sky, about half a degree wide.

The gravity on the Moon is one-sixth of the Earth's gravity. It means that an object will be one-sixth as heavy on the Moon compared to Earth.

The Moon is a rocky and dusty place. It moves slowly away from the Earth at a rate of 3.8 centimeters per year due to the effect of tidal dissipation.

Some other planets also have moons or natural satellites. The giant impact hypothesis is a common explanation for how the Moon formed.

questions.q: How strong is gravity on the Moon compared to Earth?
How fast is the Moon moving away from Earth?

materials.source: Simple English Wikipedia「Moon」（版 10950172 の冒頭を抜粋）

materials.title: E-mail
materials.body:
Electronic mail (or e-mail or email) is an Internet service that allows people who have an e-mail address (accounts) to send and receive electronic letters. Those are much like postal letters, except that they are delivered much faster than snail mail when sending over long distances, and are usually free.

Like with regular mail, users may get a lot of unwanted mail. With e-mail, this is called spam. Some programs used for sending and receiving mail can detect spam and filter it out nearly completely.

questions.q: What is unwanted email called?
How is email different from postal letters?

materials.source: Simple English Wikipedia「E-mail」（版 10438437 の冒頭を抜粋）

materials.title: Sleep
materials.body:
Sleep (also called napping) is a state of resting. It happens in most animals, including humans. To sleep is to be unconscious.

During deep sleep, most of the muscles that animals can control are not active, but resting to regain the energy they need for the next time they wake up. When asleep, humans cannot tell what is happening around them. Like most animals, healthy sleep in humans most often happens at night.

When something is asleep, it cannot react like it would if it was awake. However, waking up from sleep is easier than waking up from hibernation or a coma. All mammals and birds, as well as many reptiles, amphibians and fish have a sleep cycle. In humans and many other animals, regular sleep is essential for survival.

questions.q: When does healthy sleep in humans most often happen?
Which animals have a sleep cycle, according to the text?
options: All mammals and birds, and many other animals
Only animals that live at night

materials.source: Simple English Wikipedia「Sleep」（版 10975894 の冒頭を抜粋）

materials.title: The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse
materials.body:
A Town Mouse once visited a relative who lived in the country. For lunch the Country Mouse served wheat stalks, roots, and acorns, with a dash of cold water for drink. The Town Mouse ate very sparingly, nibbling a little of this and a little of that, and by her manner making it very plain that she ate the simple food only to be polite.

After the meal the friends had a long talk, or rather the Town Mouse talked about her life in the city while the Country Mouse listened. They then went to bed in a cozy nest in the hedgerow and slept in quiet and comfort until morning. In her sleep the Country Mouse dreamed she was a Town Mouse with all the luxuries and delights of city life that her friend had described for her. So the next day when the Town Mouse asked the Country Mouse to go home with her to the city, she gladly said yes.

When they reached the mansion in which the Town Mouse lived, they found on the table in the dining room the leavings of a very fine banquet. There were sweetmeats and jellies, pastries, delicious cheeses, indeed, the most tempting foods that a Mouse can imagine. But just as the Country Mouse was about to nibble a dainty bit of pastry, she heard a Cat mew loudly and scratch at the door. In great fear the Mice scurried to a hiding place, where they lay quite still for a long time, hardly daring to breathe. When at last they ventured back to the feast, the door opened suddenly and in came the servants to clear the table, followed by the House Dog.

The Country Mouse stopped in the Town Mouse's den only long enough to pick up her carpet bag and umbrella.

"You may have luxuries and dainties that I have not," she said as she hurried away, "but I prefer my plain food and simple life in the country with the peace and security that go with it."
materials.moral: Poverty with security is better than plenty in the midst of fear and uncertainty.

questions.q: Why did the mice run and hide in the city?
What did the Country Mouse decide in the end?
options: To go back to her simple, safe life

materials.title: The Fox and the Grapes
materials.body:
A Fox one day spied a beautiful bunch of ripe grapes hanging from a vine trained along the branches of a tree. The grapes seemed ready to burst with juice, and the Fox's mouth watered as he gazed longingly at them.

The bunch hung from a high branch, and the Fox had to jump for it. The first time he jumped he missed it by a long way. So he walked off a short distance and took a running leap at it, only to fall short once more. Again and again he tried, but in vain.

Now he sat down and looked at the grapes in disgust.

"What a fool I am," he said. "Here I am wearing myself out to get a bunch of sour grapes that are not worth gaping for."

And off he walked very, very scornfully.
materials.moral: There are many who pretend to despise and belittle that which is beyond their reach.

questions.q: Why couldn't the Fox get the grapes?
What did the Fox say about the grapes at the end?
options: They were sour and not worth it

materials.title: The Lion and the Mouse
materials.body:
A Lion lay asleep in the forest, his great head resting on his paws. A timid little Mouse came upon him unexpectedly, and in her fright and haste to get away, ran across the Lion's nose. Roused from his nap, the Lion laid his huge paw angrily on the tiny creature to kill her.

"Spare me!" begged the poor Mouse. "Please let me go and some day I will surely repay you."

The Lion was much amused to think that a Mouse could ever help him. But he was generous and finally let the Mouse go.

Some days later, while stalking his prey in the forest, the Lion was caught in the toils of a hunter's net. Unable to free himself, he filled the forest with his angry roaring. The Mouse knew the voice and quickly found the Lion struggling in the net. Running to one of the great ropes that bound him, she gnawed it until it parted, and soon the Lion was free.

"You laughed when I said I would repay you," said the Mouse. "Now you see that even a Mouse can help a Lion."

questions.q: Why did the Lion let the Mouse go?
How did the Mouse help the Lion?
options: She bit through the net's rope

materials.title: The Crow and the Pitcher
materials.body:
In a spell of dry weather, when the Birds could find very little to drink, a thirsty Crow found a pitcher with a little water in it. But the pitcher was high and had a narrow neck, and no matter how he tried, the Crow could not reach the water. The poor thing felt as if he must die of thirst.

Then an idea came to him. Picking up some small pebbles, he dropped them into the pitcher one by one. With each pebble the water rose a little higher until at last it was near enough so he could drink.
materials.moral: In a pinch a good use of our wits may help us out.

questions.q: What was the Crow's problem?
options: He could not reach the water

questions.q: What did the Crow put into the pitcher?

materials.title: The Hare and the Tortoise
materials.body:
A Hare was making fun of the Tortoise one day for being so slow.

"Do you ever get anywhere?" he asked with a mocking laugh.

"Yes," replied the Tortoise, "and I get there sooner than you think. I'll run you a race and prove it."

The Hare was much amused at the idea of running a race with the Tortoise, but for the fun of the thing he agreed. So the Fox, who had consented to act as judge, marked the distance and started the runners off.

The Hare was soon far out of sight, and to make the Tortoise feel very deeply how ridiculous it was for him to try a race with a Hare, he lay down beside the course to take a nap until the Tortoise should catch up.

The Tortoise meanwhile kept going slowly but steadily, and, after a time, passed the place where the Hare was sleeping. But the Hare slept on very peacefully; and when at last he did wake up, the Tortoise was near the goal. The Hare now ran his swiftest, but he could not overtake the Tortoise in time.
materials.moral: The race is not always to the swift.

questions.q: Why did the Hare lose the race?
Who was the judge of the race?

materials.title: The North Wind and the Sun
materials.body:
The North Wind and the Sun had a quarrel about which of them was the stronger. While they were disputing with much heat and bluster, a Traveler passed along the road wrapped in a cloak.

"Let us agree," said the Sun, "that he is the stronger who can strip that Traveler of his cloak."

"Very well," growled the North Wind, and at once sent a cold, howling blast against the Traveler.

With the first gust of wind the ends of the cloak whipped about the Traveler's body. But he immediately wrapped it closely around him, and the harder the Wind blew, the tighter he held it to him. The North Wind tore angrily at the cloak, but all his efforts were in vain.

Then the Sun began to shine. At first his beams were gentle, and in the pleasant warmth after the bitter cold of the North Wind, the Traveler unfastened his cloak and let it hang loosely from his shoulders. The Sun's rays grew warmer and warmer. The man took off his cap and mopped his brow. At last he became so heated that he pulled off his cloak, and, to escape the blazing sunshine, threw himself down in the welcome shade of a tree by the roadside.
materials.moral: Gentleness and kind persuasion win where force and bluster fail.

questions.q: What test did the Wind and the Sun agree on?
options: Who could make the Traveler take off his cloak

questions.q: Why did the Traveler take off his cloak?
options: He became too hot in the sun
He gave it to a friend

materials.title: The Shepherd Boy and the Wolf
materials.body:
A Shepherd Boy tended his master's Sheep near a dark forest not far from the village. Soon he found life in the pasture very dull. All he could do to amuse himself was to talk to his dog or play on his shepherd's pipe.

One day as he sat watching the Sheep and the quiet forest, and thinking what he would do should he see a Wolf, he thought of a plan to amuse himself.

His Master had told him to call for help should a Wolf attack the flock, and the Villagers would drive it away. So now, though he had not seen anything that even looked like a Wolf, he ran toward the village shouting at the top of his voice, "Wolf! Wolf!"

As he expected, the Villagers who heard the cry dropped their work and ran in great excitement to the pasture. But when they got there they found the Boy doubled up with laughter at the trick he had played on them.

A few days later the Shepherd Boy again shouted, "Wolf! Wolf!" Again the Villagers ran to help him, only to be laughed at again.

Then one evening as the sun was setting behind the forest and the shadows were creeping out over the pasture, a Wolf really did spring from the underbrush and fall upon the Sheep.

In terror the Boy ran toward the village shouting "Wolf! Wolf!" But though the Villagers heard the cry, they did not run to help him as they had before. "He cannot fool us again," they said.

The Wolf killed a great many of the Boy's sheep and then slipped away into the forest.
materials.moral: Liars are not believed even when they speak the truth.

questions.q: Why did the Boy first shout 'Wolf! Wolf!'?
Why didn't the Villagers help the last time?
options: They thought he was lying again
They were afraid of the Wolf

materials.title: Aesop: The Wolf and the Kid / The Tortoise and the Ducks / The Young Crab and his Mother / The Frogs and the Ox
materials.body:
The Wolf and the Kid

There was once a little Kid whose growing horns made him think he was a grown-up Billy Goat and able to take care of himself. So one evening when the flock started home from the pasture and his mother called, the Kid paid no heed and kept right on nibbling the tender grass. A little later when he lifted his head, the flock was gone.

He was all alone. The sun was sinking. Long shadows came creeping over the ground. A chilly little wind came creeping with them making scary noises in the grass. The Kid shivered as he thought of the terrible Wolf. Then he started wildly over the field, bleating for his mother. But not half-way, near a clump of trees, there was the Wolf!

The Kid knew there was little hope for him.

"Please, Mr. Wolf," he said trembling, "I know you are going to eat me. But first please pipe me a tune, for I want to dance and be merry as long as I can."

The Wolf liked the idea of a little music before eating, so he struck up a merry tune and the Kid leaped and frisked gaily.

Meanwhile, the flock was moving slowly homeward. In the still evening air the Wolf's piping carried far. The Shepherd Dogs pricked up their ears. They recognized the song the Wolf sings before a feast, and in a moment they were racing back to the pasture. The Wolf's song ended suddenly, and as he ran, with the Dogs at his heels, he called himself a fool for turning piper to please a Kid, when he should have stuck to his butcher's trade.

Moral: Do not let anything turn you from your purpose.

The Tortoise and the Ducks

The Tortoise, you know, carries his house on his back. No matter how hard he tries, he cannot leave home. They say that Jupiter punished him so, because he was such a lazy stay-at-home that he would not go to Jupiter's wedding, even when especially invited.

After many years, Tortoise began to wish he had gone to that wedding. When he saw how gaily the birds flew about and how the Hare and the Chipmunk and all the other animals ran nimbly by, always eager to see everything there was to be seen, the Tortoise felt very sad and discontented. He wanted to see the world too, and there he was with a house on his back and little short legs that could hardly drag him along.

One day he met a pair of Ducks and told them all his trouble.

"We can help you to see the world," said the Ducks. "Take hold of this stick with your teeth and we will carry you far up in the air where you can see the whole countryside. But keep quiet or you will be sorry."

The Tortoise was very glad indeed. He seized the stick firmly with his teeth, the two Ducks took hold of it one at each end, and away they sailed up toward the clouds.

Just then a Crow flew by. He was very much astonished at the strange sight and cried:

"This must surely be the King of Tortoises!"

"Why certainly----" began the Tortoise.

But as he opened his mouth to say these foolish words he lost his hold on the stick, and down he fell to the ground, where he was dashed to pieces on a rock.

Moral: Foolish curiosity and vanity often lead to misfortune.

The Young Crab and his Mother

"Why in the world do you walk sideways like that?" said a Mother Crab to her son. "You should always walk straight forward with your toes turned out."

"Show me how to walk, mother dear," answered the little Crab obediently, "I want to learn."

So the old Crab tried and tried to walk straight forward. But she could walk sideways only, like her son. And when she wanted to turn her toes out she tripped and fell on her nose.

Moral: Do not tell others how to act unless you can set a good example.

The Frogs and the Ox

An Ox came down to a reedy pool to drink. As he splashed heavily into the water, he crushed a young Frog into the mud. The old Frog soon missed the little one and asked his brothers and sisters what had become of him.

"A great big monster," said one of them, "stepped on little brother with one of his huge feet!"

"Big, was he!" said the old Frog, puffing herself up. "Was he as big as this?"

"Oh, much bigger!" they cried.

The Frog puffed up still more.

"He could not have been bigger than this," she said. But the little Frogs all declared that the monster was much, much bigger and the old Frog kept puffing herself out more and more until, all at once, she burst.

Moral: Do not attempt the impossible.

questions.q: Why did the young Crab fail to learn to walk forward?
options: His mother could only walk sideways too
He did not want to learn

questions.q: What happened to the old Frog in the end?
options: She ran away from the Ox
She puffed herself up until she burst
She became bigger than the Ox

materials.source: 朗読：Bob Neufeld（LibriVox「The Aesop for Children」区切り1）／本文：The Aesop for Children（1919年）

materials.title: Aesop: The Dog, the Cock, and the Fox / Belling the Cat / The Eagle and the Jackdaw / The Boy and the Filberts
materials.body:
The Dog, the Cock, and the Fox

A Dog and a Cock, who were the best of friends, wished very much to see something of the world. So they decided to leave the farmyard and to set out into the world along the road that led to the woods. The two comrades traveled along in the very best of spirits and without meeting any adventure to speak of.

At nightfall the Cock, looking for a place to roost, as was his custom, spied nearby a hollow tree that he thought would do very nicely for a night's lodging. The Dog could creep inside and the Cock would fly up on one of the branches. So said, so done, and both slept very comfortably.

With the first glimmer of dawn the Cock awoke. For the moment he forgot just where he was. He thought he was still in the farmyard where it had been his duty to arouse the household at daybreak. So standing on tip-toes he flapped his wings and crowed lustily. But instead of awakening the farmer, he awakened a Fox not far off in the wood. The Fox immediately had rosy visions of a very delicious breakfast. Hurrying to the tree where the Cock was roosting, he said very politely:

"A hearty welcome to our woods, honored sir. I cannot tell you how glad I am to see you here. I am quite sure we shall become the closest of friends."

"I feel highly flattered, kind sir," replied the Cock slyly. "If you will please go around to the door of my house at the foot of the tree, my porter will let you in."

The hungry but unsuspecting Fox, went around the tree as he was told, and in a twinkling the Dog had seized him.

Moral: Those who try to deceive may expect to be paid in their own coin.

Belling the Cat

The Mice once called a meeting to decide on a plan to free themselves of their enemy, the Cat. At least they wished to find some way of knowing when she was coming, so they might have time to run away. Indeed, something had to be done, for they lived in such constant fear of her claws that they hardly dared stir from their dens by night or day.

Many plans were discussed, but none of them was thought good enough. At last a very young Mouse got up and said:

"I have a plan that seems very simple, but I know it will be successful. All we have to do is to hang a bell about the Cat's neck. When we hear the bell ringing we will know immediately that our enemy is coming."

All the Mice were much surprised that they had not thought of such a plan before. But in the midst of the rejoicing over their good fortune, an old Mouse arose and said:

"I will say that the plan of the young Mouse is very good. But let me ask one question: Who will bell the Cat?"

Moral: It is one thing to say that something should be done, but quite a different matter to do it.

The Eagle and the Jackdaw

An Eagle, swooping down on powerful wings, seized a lamb in her talons and made off with it to her nest. A Jackdaw saw the deed, and his silly head was filled with the idea that he was big and strong enough to do as the Eagle had done. So with much rustling of feathers and a fierce air, he came down swiftly on the back of a large Ram. But when he tried to rise again he found that he could not get away, for his claws were tangled in the wool. And so far was he from carrying away the Ram, that the Ram hardly noticed he was there.

The Shepherd saw the fluttering Jackdaw and at once guessed what had happened. Running up, he caught the bird and clipped its wings. That evening he gave the Jackdaw to his children.

"What a funny bird this is!" they said laughing, "what do you call it, father?"

"That is a Jackdaw, my children. But if you should ask him, he would say he is an Eagle."

Moral: Do not let your vanity make you overestimate your powers.

The Boy and the Filberts

A Boy was given permission to put his hand into a pitcher to get some filberts. But he took such a great fistful that he could not draw his hand out again. There he stood, unwilling to give up a single filbert and yet unable to get them all out at once. Vexed and disappointed he began to cry.

"My boy," said his mother, "be satisfied with half the nuts you have taken and you will easily get your hand out. Then perhaps you may have some more filberts some other time."

Moral: Do not attempt too much at once.

options: To hang a bell on the Cat

questions.q: Why could the Boy not get his hand out of the pitcher?
options: He took too many filberts at once

materials.title: Aesop: The Bundle of Sticks / The Wolf and the Crane / The Ass and his Driver / The Oxen and the Wheels
materials.body:
The Bundle of Sticks

A certain Father had a family of Sons, who were forever quarreling among themselves. No words he could say did the least good, so he cast about in his mind for some very striking example that should make them see that discord would lead them to misfortune.

One day when the quarreling had been much more violent than usual and each of the Sons was moping in a surly manner, he asked one of them to bring him a bundle of sticks. Then handing the bundle to each of his Sons in turn he told them to try to break it. But although each one tried his best, none was able to do so.

The Father then untied the bundle and gave the sticks to his Sons to break one by one. This they did very easily.

"My Sons," said the Father, "do you not see how certain it is that if you agree with each other and help each other, it will be impossible for your enemies to injure you? But if you are divided among yourselves, you will be no stronger than a single stick in that bundle."

Moral: In unity is strength.

The Wolf and the Crane

A Wolf had been feasting too greedily, and a bone had stuck crosswise in his throat. He could get it neither up nor down, and of course he could not eat a thing. Naturally that was an awful state of affairs for a greedy Wolf.

So away he hurried to the Crane. He was sure that she, with her long neck and bill, would easily be able to reach the bone and pull it out.

"I will reward you very handsomely," said the Wolf, "if you pull that bone out for me."

The Crane, as you can imagine, was very uneasy about putting her head in a Wolf's throat. But she was grasping in nature, so she did what the Wolf asked her to do.

When the Wolf felt that the bone was gone, he started to walk away.

"But what about my reward!" called the Crane anxiously.

"What!" snarled the Wolf, whirling around. "Haven't you got it? Isn't it enough that I let you take your head out of my mouth without snapping it off?"

Moral: Expect no reward for serving the wicked.

The Ass and his Driver

An Ass was being driven along a road leading down the mountain side, when he suddenly took it into his silly head to choose his own path. He could see his stall at the foot of the mountain, and to him the quickest way down seemed to be over the edge of the nearest cliff. Just as he was about to leap over, his master caught him by the tail and tried to pull him back, but the stubborn Ass would not yield and pulled with all his might.

"Very well," said his master, "go your way, you willful beast, and see where it leads you."

With that he let go, and the foolish Ass tumbled head over heels down the mountain side.

Moral: They who will not listen to reason but stubbornly go their own way against the friendly advice of those who are wiser than they, are on the road to misfortune.

The Oxen and the Wheels

A pair of Oxen were drawing a heavily loaded wagon along a miry country road. They had to use all their strength to pull the wagon, but they did not complain.

The Wheels of the wagon were of a different sort. Though the task they had to do was very light compared with that of the Oxen, they creaked and groaned at every turn. The poor Oxen, pulling with all their might to draw the wagon through the deep mud, had their ears filled with the loud complaining of the Wheels. And this, you may well know, made their work so much the harder to endure.

"Silence!" the Oxen cried at last, out of patience. "What have you Wheels to complain about so loudly? We are drawing all the weight, not you, and we are keeping still about it besides."

Moral: They complain most who suffer least.

questions.q: What did the Father want his Sons to learn from the sticks?
options: That they are strong when they stay together

questions.q: Why were the Oxen angry with the Wheels?
options: The Wheels complained although their work was light
The Wheels broke in the mud
